_doc: How each masonry material behaves, as numbers: engine-neutral (the portability rule, destruction-spec.md section 1). Salt Creek's code reads these; nothing here is Godot's. Every number is a FIRST GUESS (step 1 of the masonry lab) until a step tunes it against the reference library and Sean's eye; 'status' says which. Strengths are failure values (what breaks it), not the cautious design values an engineer sizes by, as TimberTuning's are. Field meanings are in destruction-spec.md section 3. Units: SI throughout (kg, m, Pa, J, s); sizes are [length along the wall, height, depth through the wall].
status: first guess, 2026-11-04 (masonry lab step 1); material list approved by Sean (#666, 2026-11-04)

solver._doc: Dials for the rules in destruction-spec.md sections 5 and 6, the same for every material.

lime._doc: Non-hydraulic lime putty and sand, 1:3, as laid in the 1880s West (Portland cement was imported and dear until the 1890s). Weak and soft on purpose: the joint is the weak link, which is what makes masonry break along its mortar.

mud._doc: The adobe's own soil, laid wet as mortar: bond barely more than the dried mud's grip.

adobe.name: Adobe (sun-dried mud brick)
adobe.where: Older houses, outbuildings, yard walls. Normandy: cob and mud infill.

unit._doc: Sun-dried, straw-tempered soil brick, the New Mexico size (10 x 14 x 4 in).

element._doc: The solver's piece: one adobe. A 4 x 3 m panel 0.6 thick is ~550 of them.

rubble_stone.name: Rubble stone in lime mortar
rubble_stone.where: The jail, the powder magazine, retaining walls, the back walls of stores. Normandy: farmhouses, barns, field walls.

unit._doc: Field or quarry stone roughly squared with a hammer (coursed rubble), local sandstone. The wall as a whole is far weaker than its stones: the joints are thick and irregular.

element._doc: One stone. A 4 x 3 m panel 0.55 thick is ~300.

cut_stone.name: Cut (dressed) stone, ashlar
cut_stone.where: The bank's front, bridge piers, quoins, lintels and sills. Normandy: church walls, chateaux, door surrounds.

unit._doc: Sandstone dressed square, 2 x 1 x 1 ft, laid in thin lime joints.

element._doc: One block. A 4 x 3 m panel is ~70 blocks (with a rubble backing behind if thick).

cut_stone.never: A dressed wall shattering like glass.

fired_brick.name: Fired brick in lime mortar
fired_brick.where: The bank's front, better commercial buildings, chimneys. Normandy: brick houses, chimneys, infill.

unit._doc: Soft-to-medium fired common brick, 8 x 3 3/4 x 2 1/4 in, the 1880s American size.

element._doc: The solver's piece is a clump, not a brick: 2 bricks along x 4 courses high (8 a wythe) breaks off as one, still mortared, and comes apart into its bricks when it lands hard (the 'How it should break' table). A brick each would be ~3,000 elements a panel.

timber_in_masonry.name: Timber in masonry (lintels, joists, beams, plates)
timber_in_masonry.where: Lintels over openings, floor joists and roof beams bearing on stone walls. Normandy: colombage (half-timbering), floors and roofs.

timber._doc: Rough-sawn, air-dried western softwood: the same numbers as Salt Creek's 'framing' wood (config/timber.tres, from the USDA Wood Handbook). The game's TimberTuning is its source while the lab runs; a test holds the two the same.

small_hit._doc: Splinters and gouges: the game's voxel carving of wood, unchanged.

big_hit._doc: Snaps along the grain with long splinters (the game's timber cut and break, unchanged); the masonry above loses its support and the arch rule decides what falls.

timber_in_masonry.never: A beam vanishing, or snapping cleanly.

sources.baker_1889: Ira O. Baker, A Treatise on Masonry Construction (1889): period US practice: rubble, ashlar and brick walls, wall thicknesses, lintels and their bearing, arches.
sources.heyman_1995: Jacques Heyman, The Stone Skeleton (1995): masonry has no useful tension, ample compression, and doesn't slide; stability is geometry (the thrust line inside the masonry).
sources.lourenco_1996: Paulo B. Lourenco, Computational Strategies for Masonry Structures (TU Delft thesis, 1996): unit and joint failure, joint tension, cohesion and friction (~0.6-0.75).
sources.en1996: EN 1996-1-1 (Eurocode 6): masonry's initial shear strength (~0.1-0.3 MPa by mortar) and joint friction; used for ranges only.
sources.gillmore_1863: Q. A. Gillmore, A Practical Treatise on Limes, Hydraulic Cements and Mortars (1863): what lime mortars of the period were and how strong they got.
sources.getty_gsap: Tolles, Kimbro, Webster and Ginell, the Getty Seismic Adobe Project reports (Getty Conservation Institute, 2000-2002): how historic adobe walls crack and fail.
sources.nm_earthen_code: New Mexico Earthen Building Materials Code (14.7.4 NMAC): adobe at least 300 psi (2.1 MPa) in compression and 50 psi (0.34 MPa) modulus of rupture; old adobe often less.
sources.bia_tn10: Brick Industry Association, Technical Note 10 (dimensioning brick masonry); historic US brick sizes.
sources.bia_tn31b: Brick Industry Association, Technical Note 31B (lintels): arching action over an opening and the 45-degree load triangle.
sources.usda_wood_handbook: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: clear-wood strengths, cut down for rough stock (as config/timber.tres).
